title: Social Contract Theory
body:
**Social contract theory** treats moral rules as an agreement rational people would accept for
mutual benefit. An action is wrong when it violates a rule that everybody, acting in their own
interest, would have agreed to in advance.

It transfers to a digital setting more directly than the other two frameworks, because the
agreements are literally written down. A terms-of-service document, a privacy policy, an
end-user licence and a platform's community standards are all contracts, and the framework asks
a question about each of them: could a rational person, understanding what it says, have agreed
to it?

That question is what separates legal consent from meaningful consent. Clicking accept is
consent in a legal sense. A forty-page document written to be unread, presented at the moment a
service becomes necessary, with no alternative supplier, is consent no rational person could
have given informedly, which is the standard case in [[Data Privacy]].

The framework also handles a question the other two struggle with, which is what obligations a
platform has to people who never signed anything. Somebody discussed on a service they do not
use never entered the contract, and their interests are still affected.

[[Utilitarianism]] and [[Kantianism]] are the usual comparisons in an
[[Ethical Analysis]].
